Small Worlds

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In Gqeberha, a 90-year-old woman creates tiny, enchanting worlds by hand

Unique Selling Point:
Anne Whitefield is 90 years old, and still obsessed with the magic and nostalgia of dollhouses.

Summary:
Behind an unassuming door in Gqeberha lies a world of quiet wonder. Here, 90-year-old Anne Whitefield spends her days building miniature homes - each one filled with hand-cut wallpaper, delicately placed furniture, and the kind of detail that makes you lean in closer, just to be sure your eyes aren’t playing tricks on you.

At first glance, it’s charming. Sweet, even. But the deeper you look, the more these tiny rooms begin to feel like something else entirely - little pockets of calm, carefully made and lovingly kept.

Anne doesn’t rush. She doesn’t use kits. Some of her creations take years - even decades - to complete. And yet, she returns to them with the same gentle patience, shaping worlds small enough to fit in your hands, but rich enough to hold your attention completely.

She’s not alone. Anne is part of The Little Steps, a group of 26 women in Summerstrand who meet every two weeks to share their work, swap miniature treasures, and indulge in a shared delight for the tiniest of details. There’s laughter, a touch of competition, and a quiet pride in getting things just right.
Together, they remind us that creativity doesn’t have to be loud or grand to be meaningful. Sometimes, it lives in the smallest gestures - a perfectly placed curtain, a carefully made chair, a room that exists simply because someone loved making it.

This is a story about joy, patience, and the gentle magic of making something - no matter how small - beautifully.

SMALL WORLDS: FINAL:

GOVAN VO: There’s something unusual about this place…

GOVAN VO: Everything feels carefully preserved, untouched by time.

GOVAN VO: In these rooms, every detail has been considered.

GOVAN VO: And then you realise… none of it is life-sized.

GOVAN VO: Inside one home in Gqeberha, entire miniature worlds have been built by hand… One tiny detail at a time.



GOVAN VO: This is Anne Whitfield.

GOVAN VO: For decades, the 90-year-old retired teacher has been creating intricate dollhouses inspired by history, architecture, and memory.

ANNE WHITFIELD: “I’ve always liked little things. And I had an aunt who used to have little dolls. And if we were sick, she’d give us her dolls to play with. So I got to love the little dolls. Not, not the big ones.”

GOVAN VO: For a while, the tiny worlds gave way to a much bigger life.

ANNE WHITFIELD: “As we grew older, never thought about it. You know, we just finished school, went to college, taught for a few years, got married. Went to live on a trading station in the Transkei. And we had a wonderful life there.”

GOVAN VO: Years later, in the mid-80’s, one newspaper article changed everything.

ANNE WHITFIELD: “I saw an article in the paper, I think that was what kickstarted me. And it was a girl in East London - Bev Edelman - she is well known in sort of well-known in dollshouse circles. I didn't know her from Adam, but I phoned.”
GOVAN: “Why did you phone?”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “I said, you know, all my life I've wanted to do little things. And now I see you have a lot of little things. And she said, well, come and see.”
GOVAN: “And then?”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “Oh, I was gobsmacked. Her stuff was beautiful.”

GOVAN VO: Under Bev’s guidance, Anne’s tiny creations slowly transformed into enchanting little worlds.
ANNE WHITFIELD: “I just enjoy the decorating. I don’t want to even make one - I’ll buy the shell. And then I will attend to the inside. You wallpaper, you paint, you decide how you going to decorate, decide what you going to do. Whether you going to do Victorian or Georgian - right through the ages.”
GOVAN: “So it’s a sort of interior decoration.”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “Yes. But then I started reading up historically.”
GOVAN: “Like a history lesson?”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “Yes, and I hated history at school.”

GOVAN VO: Even now, Anne is still building, painting, and decorating…
Although the work has become harder with age.

ANNE WHITFIELD: “Well ya, I’m besotted. I can’t understand why I still want to do it because it’s an effort now.”
GOVAN: “What do you mean?”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “Well, I shake, so you try and paint the picture if you shaking and the pictures that big.”

GOVAN VO: Anne’s dollhouse collection now occupies an entire room in her house.

GOVAN VO: In this room, the magic isn’t in the size. It’s in the details you almost miss.

GOVAN LINK: “The scale of these creations is completely overwhelming. It’s almost like you don’t know where to look. But if you lean in, you start to notice the details, the intricacies that make it special. Like bunnies having a garden party on top of a table where the dolls are having a tea party, and then you realize it’s an entire theme.”

GOVAN: “Oh, you got paintings on the walls as well?”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “Yeah, well, I paint as you know. And I’ve covered the bed, but I bought the bed.”
GOVAN: “Ya but, you also have, like, the proper, proper curtains there with the window…”

GOVAN VO: This room has a kind of joy that’s hard to keep to yourself…
So I called my seven-year-old daughter, Azania, for a quick tour.

GOVAN: “Hey, how are you? Look, look, are you looking? Are you looking?
AZANIA WHITTLES: Yeah! So big!
GOVAN: Look at how big it is.
ANNE WHITFIELD: Oh, that’s so sweet.
AZANIA WHITTLES: “Wait… Is that a library?”
GOVAN: Yeah, it is! Look at it! It’s a dollhouse library!”

GOVAN VO: It turns out miniature worlds have a way of making grown adults emotional… and overenthusiastic gift-givers.

GOVAN: “This is incredibly embarrassing now, but we brought something which does not fit in any of this, but I'll just give it to you as a gift.”
GOVAN: “It's a little Carte Blanche TV. Do you see it?”

GOVAN VO: While we were lucky enough to get hands-on with Anne’s creations… her great-grandchildren know better. Around here, it’s strictly look-don’t-touch.

GOVAN: “And you say the kids are not allowed to play with this?”
ANNE WHITFIELD: “Can you blame me? They allowed to sweep without touching.”

GOVAN LINK: “This room may be Alice in Wonderland, but over there there’s a classic Dutch house and there’s a Victorian one. This is art on a different scale. Not bigger. Smaller, but still valuable in a way that I can’t quantify.”

GOVAN VO: The magic is in the detail. And Anne has spent decades perfecting it.

GOVAN VO:
What started as matchbox beds and sofas for her children, now involves delicate clay work, hand-stitched fabrics, and miniature frames cast from her own moulds.

GOVAN VO: Anne soon discovered she wasn’t alone in her obsession.

GOVAN VO: For 25 years, a group called the ‘Little Steps’ has met every second Saturday in nearby Fernglen.

GOVAN VO: Part workshop. Part social club - for people who care deeply about tiny furniture.

GOVAN: “Where’s the home of miniature art? Is it England.”
LORRAINE ALLEN: “I think England, Europe. It started off in Germany…
In the early days, the mothers used to teach their young girls to manage a mansion… by using the dolls houses.”
GOVAN: That’s where miniature art started?
LORRAINE ALLEN: “And that’s where it actually started.”

GOVAN VO: Chairperson Lorraine Allen says the trick is making every detail feel real.

GOVAN VO: Simple in theory. Much harder in practice… at least for me. After one failed attempt at making a miniature book, I decided to stick to journalism.

GOVAN: “What’s the challenge? Is it to see how small you can go?”
LORRAINE ALLEN: “No. To see how realistic you can make it.”

GOVAN VO: It may look old-fashioned, but miniature-making is evolving with the times.

GOVAN: “So this I suppose is the future of miniatures, yeah.”
LORRAINE ALLEN: “Yes. The 3D printing definitely is. Yeah. That's where it's going to go.”
GOVAN: “This looks scarily realistic.”
LORRAINE ALLEN: “And that's the beauty of it.”
GOVAN: “Do you guys compete? It seems like… you know who’s the best miniature maker in this room, right? You’re not saying it now.”
LORRAINE ALLEN: “I’m not going to say it.”



GOVAN VO: Even after decades of miniature-making, Anne is still finding new corners to fill… and tiny treasures to hold onto.

ANNE WHITFIELD: When I’m there I’m concentrating on what I'm doing and what I'm worrying about. It’s very good for me. It's my happy place.

FTB.
